title: Khalid ibn al-Walid
hook: the commander whose horsemen turned Uhud against the Muslims, later fighting for them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Ubaydah, the one the Prophet sent when a people asked for someone they could trust. Your line was: trustworthy of the ummah. Which small promise did you keep without being reminded? Day eight hundred forty-three.

Go back to the hillside at Uhud. The Muslims seem to be winning. The archers posted on a hill to guard the rear see the enemy running, leave their post, and come down for the spoils. The Qur'an, in the surah called the Family of Imran, speaks of that moment: some wanted this world, and the tide turned. Who turned it? The biographies name the man leading the Meccan horsemen, who saw the empty hill and rode around behind the Muslim lines. His name was Khalid ibn al-Walid. Today: the man who broke the Muslims at Uhud, and what he did next.
screen: `THE ARCHERS LEAVE THE HILL.` → `HORSEMEN AROUND THE BACK.` → `KHALID IBN AL-WALID.`

segments.voice: Uhud cost the Muslims dearly. Companions we have met on this road died there: Mus'ab with his short cloak, and others. Khalid's charge is part of that story. Later, the biographies say, Khalid came to Medina to become Muslim. Put yourself in that community the day he walked in. This is the man whose horsemen came around the hill. What does a community do with that? The answer is in what followed. Not long after, at Mu'tah, the battle where Ja'far and the other appointed leaders fell one after another, Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, telling the people in Medina what had happened. Zayd took the banner and fell. Ja'far took it and fell. Ibn Rawahah took it and fell. Then, he said, the banner was taken by one of the swords of God, and God gave them a way through. That sword was Khalid. Tradition calls him Saifullah, the sword of God. So the same man who broke the Muslim lines at Uhud is the one the Prophet named a sword of God. How? A report in Sahih Muslim gives the principle, through another Meccan who came over, Amr ibn al-As. When Amr hesitated, afraid of his past, the Prophet told him that Islam wipes out what came before it. The past is not erased from history; Uhud still happened. But it is not held against the man who turned. People change. And a community that believes that can find its sword in its old enemy.
screen: `UHUD COST THE MUSLIMS DEARLY.` · `THEN KHALID CAME TO MEDINA.` · `A SWORD OF GOD AT MU'TAH.` · `ISLAM WIPES OUT WHAT CAME BEFORE.` · then, large: `PEOPLE CHANGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: believe in someone's change. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you have filed under who they used to be. The cousin who was cruel in school. The coworker who once let you down. A parent, a friend, maybe yourself. Breathe in, and hold the old picture. Breathe out, and ask honestly: have I watched closely enough to know who they are now? You don't have to forget what happened. Just leave a door open. If you pray, you can ask good for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Saifullah, the sword of God, the title given to Khalid ibn al-Walid after the same horsemen who broke the Muslims at Uhud carried their banner at Mu'tah. Today's word.
Your line: people change. Today, give one person the chance to be who they are now, not who they were when you last decided about them. Day eight hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims teach that accepting Islam wipes out what came before it, and the companions' stories, Khalid's among them, are told as examples of former opponents welcomed and trusted.

fork.setup: you're one of the believers in Medina. Khalid, whose horsemen broke your lines at Uhud, arrives to become Muslim. what does the community do?
options: turn him away; Uhud is too fresh.
accept him, but never trust him with anything.
welcome him, and soon trust him with the banner.
fork.reveal: he was welcomed, and at Mu'tah he took the banner. the Prophet called him one of the swords of God.

original.note: Arabic: the sword of God, the title tradition gives Khalid, from the Mu'tah report.

trapdoor: what you thought: a great general, nothing more.
what it means: the man who broke the Muslims at Uhud, welcomed when he turned, and given the banner.
what a scholar hears: Amr ibn al-As's report in Muslim: Islam wipes out what came before it.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:152 (at Uhud some wanted this world, and the tide turned)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the archers leave the hill; Khalid leads the Meccan horsemen at Uhud; his later conversion)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3757 / 4262 (Mu'tah: Zayd, Ja'far, Ibn Rawahah fell; then one of the swords of God took the banner)
Sahih Muslim 121 (Amr ibn al-As: Islam wipes out what came before it)

notes: Khalid's role at Uhud and his conversion come from the sira, not the Qur'an or Bukhari; the script says 'the biographies name...' and 'the biographies say'. 3:152 does not name him.
'Some years later' and 'not long after' are vague timing words (Khalid's conversion is usually placed before the conquest of Mecca, Mu'tah shortly after); confirm or cut.
'Saifullah... became his name' is a popular title; the hadith says 'one of the swords of God'. Confirm framing.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm.
